title: Does exponential circuit hardness derandomize amplified relational computation?
formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[
\mathsf H_{\rm circ}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathsf{FBPP}_{\log}=\mathsf{FP}.
\]
The hypothesis \(\mathsf H_{\rm circ}\) asserts that some language decidable in deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) requires Boolean circuits of size \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) at every sufficiently large input length. The relation classes are defined below on the same universe of polynomially bounded, possibly partial relations. In particular, membership in a relation need not be efficiently verifiable or even decidable.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether FBPPlog equals FP under some plausible derandomization assumption, without choosing one. The user explicitly selected exponential worst-case Boolean-circuit hardness for a language in E on 18 September 2026. That precise implication is an editorial specialization, not a conjecture attributed verbatim to the paper.
source_formulation.caption: Aaronson–Buhrman–Kretschmer, Definition 1 p.1:2, §5 pp.1:18–19 and §7 p.1:21.

why: For general search outputs there may be no efficient way to verify a candidate or combine several candidates. This tests whether strong error reduction restores deterministic simulation under a familiar circuit-hardness assumption despite that obstruction.
status_note: Uncertain for the exact chosen implication. The paper explicitly poses the broader assumption-selection question, but does not itself select this E-versus-exponential-circuit hypothesis. Bounded checks through 18 September 2026 found no verified proof or refutation of this specialization. The user explicitly selected the assumption on that date.

progress.text: The paper asks for a plausible assumption derandomizing the amplified relational class and proves the P=NP and advice consequences.

importance.reason: A conceptual boundary of hardness-versus-randomness for general search and sampling-derived relations; it separates amplification from efficient verification and avoids the known failure of the weaker FBPP notion.

sentences: The task is to find a valid output for a relation, even when validity cannot be efficiently checked.
The randomized solver must reduce its error to 2^−t in time polynomial in the input length and t.
Output lengths stay polynomial in the original input length, independently of t.
The selected hypothesis gives exponential circuit hardness to a language computable in deterministic exponential time.
The question is whether this hypothesis guarantees a uniform deterministic polynomial-time solver for every such relation.

definitions:
Fix the binary alphabet. The hypothesis \(\mathsf H_{\rm circ}\) means that there are a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), positive rational constants \(a,\beta,K\) and an integer \(n_0\) such that one deterministic multitape Turing machine decides \(L\) on every length-\(n\) input in at most \(K2^{an}\) steps, and, for every \(n\ge n_0\), no Boolean circuit with at most \(2^{\beta n}\) gates agrees with the characteristic function of \(L\) on all of \(\{0,1\}^n\). Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs over fan-in-two AND and OR and fan-in-one NOT, with unrestricted fan-out, constant bits, \(n\) input nodes and one output. Size counts gates, not input nodes or wires. The circuit family may be nonuniform. There are no oracle gates. This is worst-case circuit hardness at all large lengths, not a claim of average-case hardness built into the assumption.

A relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\{0,1\}^*\) is polynomially bounded if there is an integer \(b\ge1\) such that \(|y|\le(|x|+2)^b\) for every \((x,y)\in R\). Its domain is \(\operatorname{dom}R=\{x:\exists y\ (x,y)\in R\}\); this domain may be a proper subset of all strings. A solver must return some valid \(y\) on every input in the domain. Its answer outside the domain is unrestricted. The relation is a mathematical predicate defining success, not an oracle or an input supplied to the solver.

The relation belongs to \(\mathsf{FBPP}_{\log}\) if there are positive integers \(b,c,K\) and one randomized classical multitape Turing machine \(M\) such that, on every pair \((x,1^t)\) with integer \(t\ge1\), every execution halts within \(K(|x|+t+2)^c\) steps and outputs a string of length at most \((|x|+2)^b\), and, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}R\),
\[
\Pr[(x,M(x,1^t))\in R]\ge1-2^{-t}.
\]
Randomness consists of independent fair bits, with the work to obtain and use them included in the bound. The output-length bound is independent of \(t\). The dyadic error parameter is equivalent to requesting error \(\varepsilon\) with time polynomial in \(|x|+\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\), by rounding \(t\) upward. It does not allow a polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Any overlong unsuccessful output can be replaced by the empty string, so the stated all-execution length convention does not restrict successful solvers.

The same polynomially bounded relation belongs to \(\mathsf{FP}\) if one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(D\) halts on every \(x\) in at most \(K'(|x|+2)^{c'}\) steps, for some constants \(K',c'\), and satisfies \((x,D(x))\in R\) whenever \(x\in\operatorname{dom}R\). Thus the displayed equality asserts that every relation with the amplified randomized solver also has a deterministic solver; the reverse containment is immediate by ignoring \(t\). Restricting both class names to polynomially bounded relations avoids a mismatch caused by adding irrelevant arbitrarily long witnesses to a relation.

All programs are uniform and use no advice or oracles. Their constants and polynomial exponents may depend on \(R\), and the deterministic solver may depend on the amplified solver and the witnesses to the hardness assumption. No uniform efficient procedure transforming descriptions of relations or solvers is required. The quantifier ranges over arbitrary relations meeting the conditions, not just total NP search problems or relations with polynomial-time verification. Repeating trials and taking a majority of output strings does not generally preserve relational validity.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the implication with the stated hypothesis and relation classes. A positive answer must handle every polynomially bounded partial relation without a verification oracle. Derandomization only of decision languages, efficiently verifiable search, or randomized solvers whose error reduction costs polynomial time in 1/epsilon does not settle the target.

context_blocks.text: The paper distinguishes amplification taking polynomial time in inverse error from amplification taking polynomial time in its logarithm. It separates the former relational class from deterministic polynomial time, so the error convention is essential.

For the logarithmic-error class the paper proves deterministic simulation from P=NP and separately proves a polynomial-advice simulation by fixing a successful random tape. Neither supplies the uniform implication selected here.

The source deliberately omits efficient verification to encompass general relations arising in quantum-computation comparisons. The card preserves that scope and records its chosen circuit assumption separately from the source’s broader request.
